title: The Limits of Cantorian Completion: Diagonal Data and Catalogue Membership
content: Complete finite prefix coverage does not determine which rules occur as whole rows in a catalogue, even when the entire diagonal is fixed. Conversely, a reordering of the same rows can encode any supplied executable binary rule at all but logarithmically many flipped-diagonal positions through a given depth, while preserving every finite census and any prescribed initial rows and columns. For uniformly evaluable catalogues, locating or bounding a uniquely promised matching row has exactly the strength of the halting problem, even with the original row collection fixed. When that collection may vary and a match is not promised, deciding membership is complete at the second existential level of the arithmetical hierarchy. Adjoining each successive flipped diagonal produces strict growth at every finite round, yet the original rows and all finite-round outputs still admit one explicit indexing. These constructions separate finite coverage, diagonal data, whole-row membership and effective access. Applied to Cantor’s arguments, they identify what diagonal exclusion does not construct. A separate historical test gives a contradiction under a literal set-level reading of the closing passage of his 1891 communication, and an evaluation test rules out his real-function comparison under total, name-independent Cauchy-name access.
